glossary.definition: The complex plane is the ordinary coordinate plane with the point (x, y) representing the number x + iy.
A complex function assigns one complex output to each allowed complex input. Writing f = u + iv separates its real and imaginary outputs.
The domain of a function is its set of allowed inputs. In complex analysis, a domain also commonly means a nonempty open connected subset of the complex plane; the context distinguishes these uses.
A neighbourhood of z₀ here is an open disk centred at z₀: all points whose distance from z₀ is less than some positive radius.
A punctured neighbourhood is an open disk with its centre removed. It describes nearby inputs without requiring the value at the centre.
An accumulation point of a set is a point with other set members arbitrarily close to it. Limits are considered at such points, using inputs from the function's domain.
The modulus of x + iy is its distance from zero, √(x² + y²). The distance between z and w is |z − w|.
The real part of x + iy is the real number x, its horizontal coordinate.
The imaginary part of x + iy is the real number y, its vertical coordinate. It is y, rather than iy.
A complex limit is the single output value approached when the input approaches a specified point from every allowed direction and path.
A path is a continuous route through a set of points, described by a parameter. Different paths can be used to disprove a proposed limit.
The epsilon–delta definition specifies a limit by an input tolerance δ for every requested output tolerance ε. The guarantee applies to all sufficiently close allowed inputs.
A sequence is an ordered list indexed by positive integers. A convergent sequence has terms that eventually remain within any prescribed distance of its limit.
Continuity at a point means the function's limit there equals its actual value. Close enough inputs then produce outputs close to that value.
Composition means feeding the output of one function into another: (f ∘ g)(z) = f(g(z)).
A complex polynomial is a finite sum of nonnegative integer powers of z multiplied by complex coefficients.
A rational function is a quotient of two polynomials, defined where its denominator is nonzero.
A closed set contains all limits of convergent sequences drawn from it. In the plane this means it contains its boundary points.
A bounded set fits inside some disk or ball of finite radius. This describes the inputs, rather than the size of a function's outputs.
In a finite-dimensional Euclidean space, a compact set is a closed and bounded set. A continuous real-valued function on a nonempty compact set attains its extrema.
A bounded function has outputs whose moduli or norms share one finite upper bound throughout the specified input set.
The triangle inequality states that the length of a sum cannot exceed the sum of the lengths: |z + w| ≤ |z| + |w|.
A complex derivative is the limit of the output increment divided by the complex input increment, with the same value for every way the increment tends to zero.
A difference quotient is a change in function value divided by the corresponding nonzero change in input. Its limit defines a derivative.

Complex differentiability at a point means its complex derivative exists there. For a real multivariable function, differentiability means a linear approximation with an error negligible relative to the input displacement.
The complex conjugate of x + iy is x − iy, obtained by reflecting the point across the real axis.
The chain rule differentiates a composition by multiplying the derivative of the outer function at the inner output by the derivative of the inner function.
Analyticity at a complex point means differentiability throughout some open disk around that point. Analyticity on an open set means differentiability at every point of that set.
An entire function is a complex function analytic on the whole complex plane.
In the isolated examples here, a singularity is an excluded or nonanalytic point around which the function is analytic on a punctured neighbourhood.
The Cauchy–Riemann equations are the pair uₓ = vᵧ and uᵧ = −vₓ relating the real and imaginary parts of a complex-differentiable function.
A partial derivative is a derivative with respect to one input coordinate while the other coordinates are held fixed.
C¹ describes a function whose first-order partial derivatives exist and are continuous on the specified open set.
C² describes a function whose partial derivatives through order two exist and are continuous on the specified open set.
A necessary condition must hold whenever the conclusion holds. Its failure rules out the conclusion; its truth alone may not establish it.
A sufficient condition guarantees a conclusion when its stated hypotheses hold.
The gradient of a real scalar function is the column of its first partial derivatives. Its dot product with a displacement gives the first-order change.
A stationary point of a differentiable scalar function is a point where every first partial derivative is zero, so its tangent approximation has no first-order change.
A local minimum is a point whose function value is no larger than values at all sufficiently close feasible points.
A strict local minimum has a smaller function value than every distinct sufficiently close feasible point.
A local maximum is a point whose function value is no smaller than values at all sufficiently close feasible points.
A saddle point here is a stationary point with both larger and smaller function values arbitrarily nearby.
An interior point has a whole open ball around it contained in the set. Small displacements in every direction are allowed.
A boundary point has points of the set and points outside it arbitrarily close to it.
Least squares chooses parameters to minimize the sum of squared residuals between a linear model's outputs and the target data.
A residual is a model output minus its corresponding target. For Ax approximating b, the residual vector is Ax − b.
The normal equations are AᵀAx = Aᵀb, the stationarity equations for minimizing the squared residual norm of Ax − b.
The Hessian of a scalar function is the square matrix of its second partial derivatives. It describes how its gradient changes and supplies the quadratic term in Taylor's theorem.
A mixed partial is a second derivative taken with respect to two different coordinates, such as fₓᵧ.
A real symmetric matrix equals its transpose: entries reflected across its main diagonal are equal.
A quadratic form is a scalar expression hᵀMh built from a vector h and a matrix M. For symmetric M it measures signed curvature in direction h.
A scalar function has a single real number as its output, even when its input is a vector.
The line segment joining a and b consists of the points (1 − t)a + tb with 0 ≤ t ≤ 1.
For a differentiable real scalar function along a segment, the mean value theorem equates its total change to one intermediate gradient dotted with the endpoint displacement.
Taylor's theorem expresses a function's change using its derivatives at a base point and a controlled remainder. The second-order version includes linear and quadratic terms.
A remainder r(h) is o(‖h‖²) when r(h)/‖h‖² tends to zero as h tends to zero through nonzero displacements.
An eigenvalue λ is a scalar for which Mv = λv has a nonzero vector solution. The matrix scales that eigenvector without changing its line.
An eigenvector of a matrix is a nonzero vector mapped to a scalar multiple of itself.
A real orthogonal matrix Q satisfies QᵀQ = I. It preserves Euclidean lengths and changes between orthonormal coordinate systems.
A real symmetric matrix is positive definite when hᵀMh > 0 for every nonzero h. Equivalently, every eigenvalue is positive.
A real symmetric matrix is negative definite when hᵀMh < 0 for every nonzero h. Equivalently, every eigenvalue is negative.
A real symmetric matrix is positive semidefinite when hᵀMh ≥ 0 for every h. Zero curvature in some nonzero directions is allowed.
A real symmetric matrix is negative semidefinite when hᵀMh ≤ 0 for every h.
A real symmetric matrix is indefinite when its quadratic form takes both positive and negative values. Its eigenvalues include both signs.
The determinant is a scalar associated with a square matrix. For a 2×2 matrix with rows (a,b) and (c,d), it is ad − bc.
An affine set contains the whole line through any two of its points, extending beyond the endpoints in both directions.
An affine combination is a weighted sum of points whose real coefficients add to one. Coefficients may be negative.
The affine hull of a set is the smallest affine set containing it, formed from all finite affine combinations of its points.
A convex set contains the whole line segment between any two of its points. Travelling straight between its points never leaves the set.
A convex combination is a weighted sum with nonnegative coefficients adding to one.
The convex hull of a set is the smallest convex set containing it, formed from all finite convex combinations of its points.
A cone is a set closed under multiplication by nonnegative scalars. With this convention a nonempty cone contains zero. A cone need not be convex.
A convex cone is a set closed under sums of nonnegative multiples of its points, combining the cone and convex-set properties.
A conic combination is a weighted sum with nonnegative coefficients, with no requirement that they add to one.
The relative interior is a set's interior when distance is measured within its affine hull, rather than in the whole surrounding space.
A hyperplane is a set aᵀx = b with nonzero a. It is a line in two dimensions and a plane in three.
A closed halfspace is one side of a hyperplane together with its boundary, written aᵀx ≤ b with nonzero a.
A polyhedron is the solution set of finitely many linear inequalities and equalities; it is an intersection of halfspaces and hyperplanes.
A closed norm ball consists of points within a fixed distance of a centre, measured using a specified norm.
A simplex is the convex hull of affinely independent points, such as a segment, triangle or tetrahedron.
A norm is a nonnegative measure of a vector's length that is zero only at zero, scales by the scalar's absolute value, and obeys the triangle inequality.
The intersection of sets contains exactly the points belonging to every one of those sets.
The union of sets contains the points belonging to at least one of those sets.
An affine map has the form F(x) = Ax + b, a linear transformation followed by a translation.
The image F(S) is the set of outputs F(x) obtained from inputs x in S.
The inverse image F⁻¹(C) is the set of all inputs mapped into C. It does not require F to have an inverse function.
A coordinate projection keeps selected coordinates and drops the others. It is a linear map, so it preserves convexity of images.
The Minkowski sum C + D consists of all x + y with x in C and y in D.
The Cartesian product C × D consists of pairs (x,y) with x in C and y in D.
The perspective map divides a vector by its positive last coordinate: P(x,t) = x/t for t > 0.
A linear-fractional map is an affine numerator divided by a positive affine denominator: (Ax + b)/(cᵀx + d), restricted to cᵀx + d > 0.
A proper cone is a convex, closed cone with nonempty interior and no line through the origin contained in it except the zero point.
A cone is solid when it has nonempty interior in the ambient vector space.
A cone is pointed when it contains no nonzero vector together with its negative. Equivalently, it contains no whole nonzero line.
A generalized inequality compares vectors using a proper cone K: x ≼ₖ y means the difference y − x belongs to K.
A partial order is a comparison relation that is reflexive, antisymmetric and transitive. Some pairs may be incomparable.
Componentwise order compares matching coordinates: x ≼ y when xᵢ ≤ yᵢ for every i.
Loewner order compares real symmetric matrices: X ≼ Y when Y − X is positive semidefinite. It is not entrywise comparison.
A minimum element of a set is a member no larger than every other member under the specified order. If it exists, it is unique.
A minimal element is a member with no distinct member below it under the specified order. Several incomparable minimal elements can coexist.
A maximum element is a member no smaller than every other member under the specified order. If it exists, it is unique.
A maximal element is a member with no distinct member above it under the specified order.
A total order is a partial order in which every pair of elements is comparable, as with ordinary real-number order.
In this deck a real vector is an ordered list of real coordinates, such as (x,y). It represents a point or displacement in a Euclidean space.
A matrix is a rectangular array of numbers. An m×n matrix has m rows and n columns and acts on n-coordinate column vectors.
The transpose interchanges a matrix's rows and columns. The transpose of a column vector is a row vector.
The dot product of two real coordinate vectors is the sum of their matching-coordinate products. It produces one scalar.
The Jacobian of a vector-valued function is the matrix with one row of first partial derivatives for each output component.
An invertible square matrix has a two-sided matrix inverse, so its associated linear equation has a unique solution for every right-hand side.
A matrix has rank deficiency when its rank is smaller than the largest possible rank. For least squares, dependent columns make AᵀA singular.
The real symmetric spectral theorem states that a real symmetric matrix has an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors and is diagonalised by an orthogonal matrix.
Vectors are orthonormal when they each have unit length and every distinct pair has zero dot product.
A global minimum is a feasible point whose function value is no larger than the value at every feasible point in the entire domain.
Points x₀,…,xₖ are affinely independent when the displacement vectors x₁−x₀,…,xₖ−x₀ are linearly independent.
Vectors are linearly independent when their only linear combination equal to zero has every coefficient zero.
The nonnegative orthant is the set of coordinate vectors whose every entry is at least zero.
The ambient space is the surrounding vector space in which a set is being studied. Interior and solidness depend on that choice.
The Lagrange remainder is a Taylor remainder expressed using a derivative evaluated at an intermediate point. It is unrelated to introducing a Lagrange multiplier constraint method here.
A set is connected when it cannot be separated into two disjoint nonempty relatively open pieces. An open connected subset of the plane is commonly called a domain.
The complex 0/0 rule here replaces a quotient limit by f′(z₀)/g′(z₀) when f and g are analytic at z₀, both vanish there, and g′(z₀) is nonzero.
Affine dimension is the number of independent coordinate directions in a set's affine hull. It can differ from a shape's intrinsic dimension.
An ellipsoid is a stretched and translated Euclidean ball. A nondegenerate ellipsoid is described by (x − a)ᵀP⁻¹(x − a) ≤ 1 with symmetric positive definite P.

sections.title: Complex Analysis I · Limits and continuity

sheets.title: Limits of complex functions
sheets.source: Zill & Shanahan, 3rd ed., §3.1.1, printed pp.103–110; FYUGP Semester V, Module III, Unit 11.

cards.title: Limit · one destination for every route
cards.meaning: A complex limit is the output value approached as the input gets close to a specified point, whichever allowed route it follows.
cards.picture: The input moves in a plane. Approaching from the real axis, imaginary axis, a diagonal or a curve must produce the same output destination.
cards.example: As z approaches 1 + i, z² approaches 2i. But conjugate(z)/z has different limits along the real and imaginary axes at zero.
cards.bridge: The epsilon–delta definition controls all sufficiently close inputs at once; checking a few paths cannot prove a limit.

cards.label: CA · 1 of 6 · 30 min
cards.title: What is a complex limit?
cards.body: A complex limit is one output approached from every allowed path to the input point. The point must be an accumulation point of the domain; its own function value is irrelevant.

cards.title: What does the limit statement guarantee?
cards.body: For every requested output tolerance ε > 0, one input radius δ > 0 works for all domain points with 0 < |z − z₀| < δ. The deleted centre need not be in the domain.

cards.title: Input disk, output disk
cards.body: The punctured input disk must map inside the output disk. The input radius can depend on ε, but cannot depend on which path the input takes.

cards.title: Separate the two coordinates
cards.body: Theorem 3.1.1 converts a complex limit into two genuine two-variable limits. Holding one coordinate fixed is not a substitute for those limits.

cards.title: A path test disproves a limit
cards.body: As t tends to zero through real nonzero values, the two answers disagree. Therefore conjugate(z)/z has no limit at zero.

cards.title: Even every straight line may miss a curve
cards.body: For each fixed real m, the straight-line limit is zero; on the vertical axis it is also zero. The parabolic path gives 1/2. Thus agreement of all straight-line tests still need not prove a limit.

cards.title: Use algebra only when its hypotheses hold
cards.body: Finite sums and products preserve limits. A quotient limit is the quotient of limits when the denominator limit is nonzero. Complex limits, when they exist, are unique.

cards.title: Cancel away from the deleted centre
cards.body: Factoring is valid for z ≠ i, precisely the punctured domain used in the limit. The original quotient is undefined at i; its limit still exists.

cards.title: An epsilon–delta proof for z² at 1
cards.legend: For a given \(\varepsilon>0\), control \(|z^2-1|\) by first restricting \(|z-1|<1\).

steps.note: Factor the output error.
Separate the factor measuring the input distance.

ask.q: Which factor is directly controlled by the input radius?
ask.why: The definition restricts exactly the distance |z − 1|.

steps.note: Rewrite the second factor around the same centre.

ask.q: Which estimate controls this factor near 1?
ask.why: The triangle inequality gives the needed upper bound.

steps.note: The triangle inequality gives output error ≤ B.
Then 0 < |z − 1| < δ implies |z + 1| < 3.

ask.q: Why include 1 in this minimum?
options: To restrict z to the real axis
ask.why: |z − 1| < 1 makes the uncontrolled factor uniformly smaller than 3.

ask.why: All estimates use modulus inequalities, so they hold throughout the disk.

cards.q: A function has limit 0 along both coordinate axes at the origin. What follows?
options: The full limit is not yet established
It is continuous at the origin
cards.why: Two paths can disprove a limit if they disagree, but agreement of two paths does not cover all approaches.

cards.q: Find the imaginary part of \(\lim_{z\to1+i}z^2\).
cards.why: (1 + i)² = 2i, so the imaginary part is 2.

cards.q: Which denominator limit permits the quotient limit law directly?
cards.why: Nonzero is the required condition; complex numbers need not be positive or real.

sheets.title: Continuity of complex functions
sheets.source: Zill & Shanahan §3.1.2 through Example 7, printed pp.110–113; FYUGP Unit 12.

cards.title: Continuity · the value agrees with the approach
cards.meaning: Continuity at a point means the value written at that point is exactly the value approached by nearby inputs.
cards.picture: A limit describes what happens around the centre. Continuity additionally checks that the centre exists in the domain and carries the matching value.
cards.example: The quotient (z² − 1)/(z − 1) approaches 2 at 1. Filling its missing value with 2 makes it continuous there.
cards.bridge: Continuity is checked relative to the domain. Both real and imaginary component functions must be continuous.

cards.label: CA · 2 of 6 · 24 min
cards.title: What is continuity at z₀?
cards.body: Continuity at z₀ means f(z₀) is defined and the limit of f(z) as z approaches z₀ equals f(z₀). The nearby inputs are taken from the function's domain.

cards.title: The local guarantee
cards.body: For each ε > 0 some δ > 0 works. At the centre itself the output difference is zero. A limit alone does not specify the centre's value.

cards.title: Three checks at the point
cards.body: Check that the value exists, that the nearby limit exists, and that they agree. A failure of any one of these prevents continuity at that point.

cards.title: Component criterion · Theorem 3.1.3
cards.tex: f=u+iv\text{ is continuous at }z_0\ \Longleftrightarrow\ u,v\text{ are continuous at }(x_0,y_0)
cards.body: Complex output distance controls both coordinate differences, while two small component differences control the complex distance. Thus the two descriptions of continuity agree.

cards.title: Conjugation is continuous everywhere
cards.body: Choose δ = ε. Reflection preserves distance, so conjugation is continuous at every complex point. Complex differentiability is a different question.

cards.title: Fill a removable hole correctly
cards.body: For z ≠ 1, the quotient equals z + 1. Its limit is 2, which determines the only continuous filling.

cards.title: A value cannot repair two different path limits
cards.body: No choice of c makes G continuous at zero. Its real-axis and imaginary-axis limits are 1 and −1, so the nearby limit fails before the value is considered.

cards.title: Continuity on a set
cards.body: Continuity on a set means continuity at every point of that set, using its relative domain. Omitting a point from the domain is different from assigning a wrong value there.

cards.q: A function has limit \(3-i\) at \(z_0\), but \(f(z_0)=3+i\). Which statement is true?
options: It is necessarily unbounded near z₀
cards.why: The existing limit and the assigned value disagree. This alone causes discontinuity.

cards.q: For z ≠ 2 let \(F(z)=(z^2-4)/(z-2)\). What real value of \(F(2)\) makes F continuous?
cards.why: The quotient equals z + 2 off the centre and approaches 4.

cards.q: Which statement about \(f(z)=\overline z\) is correct?
options: It is continuous on the whole plane
It is discontinuous on the imaginary axis
It is continuous only at zero
It is undefined on the real axis
cards.why: Conjugation preserves distance: |conjugate(z) − conjugate(z₀)| = |z − z₀|.

sheets.title: Continuity theorems and bounds
sheets.source: Zill & Shanahan §3.1, Theorems 3.1.4–3.1.5 through the bounding property, printed pp.113–115; FYUGP Unit 13.

cards.title: Bounded · one ceiling for every output
cards.meaning: A bounded function has outputs that all fit within one finite distance of zero over the specified input set.
cards.picture: A continuous function can stretch and bend a compact input region, but its image still fits inside a sufficiently large output disk.
cards.example: On |z| ≤ 2, the polynomial z² + 3z − i satisfies |f(z)| ≤ 4 + 6 + 1 = 11.
cards.bridge: The input region must be closed and bounded for the compactness guarantee. Continuity alone does not provide a global bound.

cards.label: CA · 3 of 6 · 22 min
cards.title: Theorem 3.1.4 · build continuous functions
cards.body: If f and g are continuous at z₀, then cf, f ± g and fg are continuous there. The quotient f/g is continuous there when g(z₀) is nonzero.

cards.title: Why the sum theorem works
cards.body: Use the limit law and then the two continuity assumptions. The resulting value is exactly (f + g)(z₀). The other algebraic rules follow similarly.

cards.title: Polynomials and rational functions
cards.body: Constants and z are continuous. Finite sums and products make every polynomial continuous on the plane. A rational function is continuous wherever its denominator is nonzero.

cards.title: What is a bounded function on R?
cards.body: A function is bounded on R when one finite constant M controls |f(z)| for every z in R. The bound must work over the entire set, rather than separately at each point.

cards.title: What does compact mean here?
cards.body: In the complex plane, compact means closed and bounded. A continuous function on a compact region has bounded modulus. Removing a boundary point can remove this guarantee.

cards.title: Why the bounding property holds
cards.body: For continuous f, its modulus is a continuous real-valued function of (x,y). On a nonempty compact region it attains a finite maximum, giving one bound for every output.

cards.title: Find an explicit bound
cards.body: This triangle-inequality estimate is a valid bound, though not necessarily the smallest possible bound. Existence and sharpness are different questions.

cards.title: Bounded input without closedness is not enough
cards.body: f is continuous throughout this open disk, but along z = 1 − 1/n its values equal n. A bounded input set does not itself force bounded outputs.

cards.title: Closed input without boundedness is not enough
cards.body: The plane is closed and f is continuous, but |f(n)| = n has no finite upper bound. The compact-region theorem requires both closedness and boundedness.

cards.q: Use the triangle inequality to complete \(|z^2-2z+4|\le M\) on \(|z|\le3\), with \(M=9+6+4\).
cards.why: Bound each term separately: |z|² ≤ 9, 2|z| ≤ 6 and the constant contributes 4.

cards.q: Which hypotheses guarantee a continuous complex function is bounded on R?
cards.why: A closed bounded set in the plane is compact; the continuous modulus has a finite maximum there.

cards.q: Where is \(1/(z^2+1)\) continuous?
options: At every point except i and −i
cards.why: Its polynomial denominator vanishes exactly at ±i, and the quotient law applies elsewhere.

sections.title: Complex Analysis I · Derivatives and analyticity

sheets.title: Differentiability and derivative rules
sheets.source: Zill & Shanahan §3.2 through Example 2, plus the differentiability–continuity implication in the same section, printed pp.121–126; FYUGP Units 14–15.

cards.title: Derivative · one linear response in every direction
cards.meaning: A complex derivative is a single complex number describing the first-order output change per unit complex input change.
cards.picture: A complex input can move horizontally, vertically or diagonally. One multiplication must describe the local response in every direction.
cards.example: For z² at z = 1 + i, the derivative is 2 + 2i. For conjugate(z), real and imaginary increments demand different multipliers.
cards.bridge: The difference quotient must have a full complex limit. Having real partial derivatives alone does not establish this.

cards.label: CA · 4 of 6 · 36 min
cards.title: What is a complex derivative?
cards.body: The derivative is the limit of the difference quotient as a nonzero complex increment tends to zero from every direction. If this limit exists, f is differentiable at the point.

cards.title: Differentiate z² from the definition
cards.legend: The increment \(h\) is complex and nonzero before the limit is taken.

steps.note: Start with the difference quotient.
Expand only the shifted square.

ask.q: Which expansion is valid for complex z₀ and h?
ask.why: The ordinary polynomial identity holds over the complex numbers.

steps.note: The unchanged values cancel.
Factor the increment from the numerator.

ask.q: Why is cancellation of h allowed here?
options: The derivative uses h ≠ 0 before the limit
ask.why: The difference quotient is evaluated on a punctured neighbourhood.

steps.note: The apparent division by zero has disappeared.
Now take the full complex limit.

ask.q: Does the simplified expression depend on the approach direction in its limit?
options: No; h tends to 0 on every route
ask.why: The term h vanishes regardless of its argument.

steps.note: The first-order multiplier is twice the base point.

ask.q: What is the derivative at z₀ = 1 + i?
ask.why: Substituting z₀ into 2z₀ gives 2 + 2i.

cards.title: Power, sum and constant rules
cards.body: For positive integers n the power rule follows from the binomial expansion of the difference quotient. A constant has derivative zero. The sum rules require the relevant derivatives to exist.

cards.title: Product and quotient rules
cards.body: Both f and g must be differentiable at the point, and the denominator must be nonzero for the quotient. Keep the minus sign and the square of g.

cards.title: What is the chain rule?
cards.body: The chain rule differentiates a composition: differentiate the outer function at the inner output, then multiply by the derivative of the inner function.

cards.title: Use the inner derivative
cards.body: The outer power contributes 3(z² + 1)², and the inner polynomial contributes 2z. Omitting 2z is the usual chain-rule error.

cards.title: A rational derivative
cards.body: The formula applies at z ≠ 1. The original function has no value at 1, so a derivative there is not part of this domain.

cards.title: Conjugation has no complex derivative
cards.body: The quotient has conflicting directional limits at every z₀. Conjugation is continuous everywhere but complex-differentiable nowhere.

cards.title: Differentiability forces continuity
cards.body: For h ≠ 0 write the output increment as a product. If the quotient tends to a finite derivative, the increment tends to zero, establishing continuity at z₀.

cards.title: One differentiable point is possible
cards.body: This proves f′(0) = 0. At a nonzero base point the directional quotient contains a term z₀·conjugate(h)/h and fails to have one limit. The function is differentiable only at zero.

cards.q: A function is complex-differentiable at z₀. Which conclusion must hold?
options: It is differentiable throughout every disk
cards.why: Differentiability implies continuity at the same point; neither entire analyticity nor zero derivative follows.

cards.q: Find the real number \(f'(1)\) for \(f(z)=(z^2+1)^3\).
cards.why: The derivative is 6z(z² + 1)²; at 1 it is 6·4 = 24.

cards.q: At which points does \(f(z)=|z|^2\) have a complex derivative?
cards.why: At zero the quotient is conjugate(h), which tends to zero. At any nonzero base point the directional limits disagree.

sheets.title: Analyticity and entire functions
sheets.source: Zill & Shanahan §3.2 after Example 2, printed pp.124–127; FYUGP Unit 15.

cards.title: Analytic · differentiable in a whole neighbourhood
cards.meaning: An analytic function is complex-differentiable throughout an open neighbourhood, rather than merely at one isolated point.
cards.picture: Place a small disk around the point. Every point inside that disk must also possess a complex derivative.
cards.example: z² is analytic everywhere. |z|² has a derivative at zero but fails the disk test around zero.
cards.bridge: An entire function passes this neighbourhood test throughout the whole complex plane.

cards.label: CA · 5 of 6 · 24 min
cards.title: What is analyticity at a point?
cards.body: Analyticity at z₀ means differentiability at every point of some open disk about z₀. A derivative only at the centre does not meet this definition.

cards.title: What is an entire function?
cards.body: An entire function is analytic on the whole complex plane. Every polynomial is entire, but a rational function may have excluded denominator zeros.

cards.title: Polynomials versus rational functions
cards.body: p is entire. r is analytic at every point except i and −i. Around any other point choose a disk small enough to avoid both denominator zeros.

cards.title: What is an isolated singularity here?
cards.body: An isolated singularity is an excluded or nonanalytic point surrounded by a punctured neighbourhood where the function is analytic. The function 1/z has such a point at zero.

cards.title: Pointwise and neighbourhood statements differ
cards.body: To disprove analyticity at a point, it is enough to show that every surrounding disk contains a point without a derivative. A derivative at the centre alone cannot establish analyticity.

cards.title: Differentiable at zero, nowhere analytic
cards.body: Its only differentiable point is zero. Every disk around zero contains nonzero points where the derivative fails. Thus f is not analytic at zero or anywhere else.

cards.title: A missing domain point still matters
cards.body: On its stated domain g equals z + 1 and is analytic. As currently defined it is not entire, because 1 is missing. Defining g(1) = 2 gives an entire extension.

cards.title: Analytic algebra and composition
cards.body: Sums, products and compositions of analytic functions are analytic wherever defined. A quotient is analytic where both functions are analytic and its denominator is nonzero.

cards.title: What is the complex L’Hôpital rule?
cards.body: For analytic f and g with f(z₀) = g(z₀) = 0 and g′(z₀) nonzero, the quotient limit is f′(z₀)/g′(z₀). This simple-zero version is Theorem 3.2.3.

cards.title: Apply L’Hôpital at a nonreal point
cards.body: Both polynomials vanish at i and the denominator derivative is 1. If instead g(z) = z² at zero, g′(0) = 0, so this theorem cannot be applied directly; a different argument is needed.

cards.title: A complex derivative is not a signed real slope
cards.body: Complex numbers have no real-style order that makes a derivative positive or negative. Increasing/decreasing tests from real scalar calculus cannot be transferred directly to a complex output.

cards.q: Which function is entire on its stated domain?
cards.why: Every polynomial is differentiable throughout the plane. The other choices fail at least one entire-function requirement.

cards.q: Why is \(|z|^2\) not analytic at zero despite \(f'(0)=0\)?
options: No surrounding disk consists entirely of differentiable points
cards.why: Analyticity requires differentiability throughout a neighbourhood, not just at one point.

cards.q: How many distinct points are excluded from the analytic domain of \(1/(z^2-4)\)?
cards.why: The denominator factors as (z − 2)(z + 2), giving two excluded points.

sheets.title: Cauchy–Riemann equations
sheets.source: Zill & Shanahan §3.3 through Theorem 3.3.2 only, printed pp.130–133; FYUGP Unit 16.

cards.title: Cauchy–Riemann · two descriptions must agree
cards.meaning: The Cauchy–Riemann equations are two matching conditions on the partial derivatives of the real and imaginary outputs.
cards.picture: Calculate the complex derivative using a horizontal increment, then a vertical increment. If one derivative exists, those answers must be identical.
cards.example: For z², u = x² − y² and v = 2xy. Their derivatives satisfy uₓ = vᵧ and uᵧ = −vₓ everywhere.
cards.bridge: The equations are necessary at a differentiable point. Continuous first partials together with the equations throughout a domain give the sufficiency theorem.

cards.label: CA · 6 of 6 · 38 min
cards.title: What are the Cauchy–Riemann equations?
cards.body: They are the pair uₓ = vᵧ and uᵧ = −vₓ for f = u + iv. Theorem 3.3.1 says they must hold at every point where a complex derivative exists.

cards.title: Why the two equations are necessary
cards.legend: Assume the full complex derivative exists at \(z=x+iy\). Then both horizontal and vertical quotient limits equal it.

steps.note: A full derivative must agree with the horizontal approach.
The two real component limits are x-partials.

ask.q: What makes these component limits legitimate?
options: The full complex derivative was assumed to exist
u and v must be constants
ask.why: Existence of the derivative forces the real and imaginary parts of the restricted quotient to converge.

steps.note: Use the vertical approach to the same derivative.

ask.q: What is the input increment on the vertical route?
ask.why: A vertical displacement t in the imaginary coordinate is the complex increment it.

steps.note: The real parameter t now defines the y-partials.
Dividing by i rotates the quotient.

ask.q: Which sign appears on the imaginary part after division by i?
ask.why: (uᵧ + ivᵧ)/i = −iuᵧ + vᵧ.

steps.note: Both expressions describe the same complex number.

ask.q: What follows by matching its two real coordinates?
ask.why: Equality of complex numbers gives equality of real parts and equality of imaginary parts.

cards.title: Check a polynomial explicitly
cards.body: Here uₓ = 2x + 1 = vᵧ, while uᵧ = −2y = −vₓ. The four partial derivatives are continuous throughout the plane.

cards.title: One failed equation rules out a derivative
cards.body: Since uₓ ≠ vᵧ at every point, this continuous function has no complex derivative anywhere. Necessity is especially useful for ruling differentiability out.

cards.title: Equations on one line do not give analyticity
cards.body: The other equation holds everywhere, but uₓ = vᵧ only on y = 2x. No open disk lies inside that line, so f is nowhere analytic, even though C¹ regularity gives differentiability at points on the line.

cards.title: Necessary is not sufficient at an isolated point
cards.body: Satisfying the two equations at one point alone does not prove a derivative there. A criterion using continuous partial derivatives on a neighbourhood supplies the missing control.

cards.title: A counterexample to a point-only test
cards.body: All four first partials at zero are zero, so the equations hold there. Yet F(h)/h is zero along the axes and 1/2 along y = x. The complex derivative fails at zero.

cards.title: Theorem 3.3.2 · criterion for analyticity
cards.body: If u and v have continuous first partial derivatives on an open domain D and satisfy both Cauchy–Riemann equations throughout D, then f = u + iv is analytic on D.

cards.title: Apply the full domain criterion
cards.body: The partials are continuous and the equations hold at every point, so f is entire. The derivative expression is the one obtained in the horizontal part of the necessity proof.

cards.title: A reliable checking order
cards.body: State the domain, identify u and v, compute all four first partials, check continuity, then test both equations on the required neighbourhood. Do not replace this by checking one coordinate axis.

cards.q: The Cauchy–Riemann equations fail at z₀. What can be concluded immediately?
options: The function has no complex derivative there
Its real partial derivatives cannot exist
cards.why: The equations are necessary for complex differentiability, but failure need not prevent continuity or real partial derivatives.
Differentiate v with respect to x, holding y fixed: vₓ = 2y = 6.

cards.q: Which data meet Theorem 3.3.2 on an open domain D?
options: Both equations at one point only
C¹ real and imaginary parts, with both equations everywhere in D
A derivative at one point of D
cards.why: The theorem requires regularity of the components and both equations throughout the domain.

sheets.title: Stationary points and conditions
sheets.source: Binmore, 2nd ed., §§19.27–19.30, printed pp.217–219; FYUGP Module I, Unit 4.

cards.title: Stationary · no first-order rise in any direction
cards.meaning: A stationary point is a point where a differentiable scalar function has a zero gradient.
cards.picture: At that point the tangent plane is horizontal. The surface may still be bowl-shaped, cap-shaped or saddle-shaped above that tangent plane.
cards.example: For f(x,y) = xy, the gradient is (y,x), so zero is stationary. Along y = x the function rises, while along y = −x it falls.
cards.bridge: Stationarity is necessary for an interior differentiable extremum, but it does not classify the point.

cards.label: CO · 1 of 8 · 20 min
cards.title: What is a stationary point?
cards.body: A stationary point is a point where all first partial derivatives of a differentiable scalar function vanish. Its first-order tangent approximation is constant.

cards.title: Column gradient, row derivative
cards.body: We use a column gradient and a row total derivative. Their entries are the same first partials. A zero row or zero column states the same stationarity condition.

cards.title: The necessary condition needs an interior point
cards.body: At an interior local minimum or maximum of a differentiable function, the gradient is zero. Restricting to every coordinate line reduces this to the one-variable extremum condition.

cards.title: A boundary minimum need not be stationary
cards.body: The minimum over the interval occurs at its boundary 0, despite the nonzero derivative of the ambient function. The interior hypothesis cannot be discarded.

cards.title: Find a candidate before classifying it
cards.body: Solving 2x + y = 4 and x + 2y = 2 gives (2,0). This is a stationary candidate; its Hessian will justify calling it a minimum later.

cards.title: Zero gradient does not imply an extremum
cards.body: The origin is stationary but is a saddle point. A one-variable example is x³ at zero: its first derivative vanishes, yet the function passes through both signs.

cards.title: What is least squares?
cards.body: Least squares chooses x to minimize the squared length of the residual Ax − b. It replaces an inconsistent system by the best fit measured in Euclidean distance.

cards.title: Derive the normal equations
cards.legend: Here \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), \(b\in\mathbb R^m\). The transpose convention matches our column gradient.

phases.name: Expand
phases.why: write the squared residual as a scalar

steps.note: A squared Euclidean norm is a dot product.
Expand the product without changing dimensions.

ask.q: What size is AᵀA?
ask.why: Aᵀ is n × m and A is m × n.

steps.note: The two cross terms are equal real scalars.

move.label: Differentiate the scalar using a column gradient

steps.note: AᵀA is symmetric, so the quadratic gradient has factor 2.

ask.q: Why does bᵀb contribute no gradient term?
ask.why: The data vector b is fixed while x varies.

steps.note: Factor the residual back into the gradient.
An unconstrained minimizer must be stationary.

ask.q: Which first-order condition is required at a minimizer?
ask.why: An inconsistent system can have a nonzero optimal residual, but the objective gradient still vanishes.

steps.note: The nonzero scalar factor is irrelevant.
Distribute the transpose factor.
These are the normal equations.

ask.q: When may we solve uniquely using (AᵀA)⁻¹?
options: Only when the residual is zero
ask.why: Invertibility is needed to write a unique inverse-based solution; rank deficiency may give multiple minimizers.

steps.note: Write the equations in their usual order.

cards.title: Fit one constant to two data values
cards.body: The stationary fit is c = 2, with residuals 1 and −1. The residual is not zero, but it is orthogonal to the model's constant direction.

cards.q: Find the stationary value of c for \(F(c)=(c-2)^2+(c-6)^2\).
cards.why: F′(c) = 4c − 16, so stationarity gives c = 4.

cards.q: Which point must satisfy the zero-gradient condition?
options: Any point with positive Hessian determinant
cards.why: The first-order necessary condition applies at an interior differentiable extremum.

cards.q: At the origin, f(x,y) = xy has zero gradient. What does this alone establish?
cards.why: The zero gradient identifies a stationary point; the opposite signs along two lines show why it does not imply a minimum.

cards.title: Hessian · a table of second-order responses
cards.meaning: A Hessian is the square matrix containing all second partial derivatives of a scalar function.
cards.picture: The gradient records first-order slopes. The Hessian records how each gradient entry changes as each input coordinate changes.
cards.example: For f = x² + xy + 2y², the gradient is (2x + y, x + 4y), and the Hessian has rows (2,1) and (1,4).
cards.bridge: The matrix produces a scalar curvature response hᵀHh in any chosen displacement direction h.

cards.label: CO · 2 of 8 · 22 min
cards.title: What is the Hessian matrix?
cards.body: The Hessian is the matrix of second partial derivatives of a scalar function. With a column gradient, it is the Jacobian of that gradient.

cards.title: Build it one row at a time
cards.body: Differentiate the first gradient component with respect to x and y for the first row; do the same for the second component for the second row.

cards.title: What are mixed partials and symmetry?
cards.body: Mixed partials differentiate in two different coordinates. A symmetric matrix equals its transpose. Continuous second partials near a point guarantee fₓᵧ = fᵧₓ there.

cards.title: Do not assume constant curvature
cards.body: At (1,2), this becomes rows (6,4) and (4,2). The Hessian generally varies with the evaluation point; a quadratic polynomial is a special constant-Hessian case.

cards.title: State the regularity hypothesis
cards.body: Continuous second partial derivatives are a sufficient condition for a symmetric Hessian. The mere existence of two iterated mixed partials does not universally guarantee their equality.

cards.title: A direction turns a matrix into one curvature
cards.body: For the constant Hessian with rows (2,1) and (1,4), the mixed term occurs twice. The second derivative along the line x = a + th is hᵀH_f(a + th)h.

cards.title: The Taylor coefficient is half the Hessian form
cards.body: For a quadratic function, this term gives the exact second-order contribution. Using hᵀHh without the factor 1/2 doubles the quadratic Taylor term.

cards.q: For \(f=x^2+xy+2y^2\), find \(f_{yy}\).
cards.why: Differentiate fᵧ = x + 4y once more with respect to y.

cards.q: For \(H=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&4\end{pmatrix}\) and \(h=(1,1)^T\), calculate \(h^THh\).
cards.why: Hh = (3,5)ᵀ, and the dot product with (1,1) is 8.

cards.q: Which hypothesis guarantees the usual equality of mixed second partials near a point?
options: The function has a zero value
The gradient vanishes at one point
The second partials exist and are continuous nearby
cards.why: Continuity of the second partials supplies the mixed-partial symmetry theorem's regularity condition.

sheets.title: Mean value and second-order Taylor
sheets.source: Binmore §§19.34–19.36, printed pp.221–223; FYUGP Unit 6, whose content line is blank in the local syllabus table but is explicitly assigned in the timetable.

cards.title: Taylor · value, tilt and curvature
cards.meaning: A second-order Taylor expansion describes a nearby function value using the base value, first-order tilt and a quadratic curvature term.
cards.picture: Walk from a to a + h along one straight segment. The multivariable problem becomes the one-variable function g(t) = f(a + th).
cards.example: For f = x² + xy + 2y² at a = 0, the value and gradient terms vanish, leaving ½hᵀHh exactly.
cards.bridge: The exact remainder evaluates the Hessian at an intermediate point. Replacing it by H(a) requires a small-o remainder.

cards.label: CO · 3 of 8 · 24 min
cards.title: What does the mean value theorem say?
cards.body: For a real scalar function continuous on a segment and differentiable along its interior, one intermediate gradient dotted with the displacement equals the total change.

cards.title: Reduce the theorem to one variable
cards.body: Apply the ordinary scalar mean value theorem to g on [0,1]. The whole segment must lie in the function's domain; differentiability can be ensured by an open neighbourhood around it.

cards.title: Find an intermediate point
cards.body: At c = (t,2t), the gradient dot (1,2) is 10t. Thus t = 1/2 gives the mean value point c = (1/2,1).

cards.title: One common vector mean value point may fail
cards.body: A common equality F(1) − F(0) = F′(c) would require 2c = 1 and 3c² = 1 simultaneously. They have no common solution. The scalar theorem does not extend to vector outputs in that form.

cards.title: What is second-order Taylor's theorem?
cards.body: It expresses a nearby scalar value as the base value plus a linear term and a quadratic remainder involving the Hessian at an intermediate point on the joining segment.

cards.title: Derive second-order Taylor along a segment
cards.legend: Assume \(f\) is C² on an open neighbourhood of the segment from \(a\) to \(a+h\). Set \(g(t)=f(a+th)\).

steps.note: The segment is traversed by 0 ≤ t ≤ 1.
Use the chain rule; h is a constant displacement.

ask.q: What is the derivative of a + th with respect to t?
ask.why: The base point is constant and the path's velocity is h.

steps.note: Differentiate the gradient along the same direction.

ask.q: Which expression is a scalar second directional derivative?
ask.why: The row–matrix–column product is a scalar and records curvature along h.

steps.note: Some t* lies strictly between 0 and 1.

ask.q: Where is the remainder's evaluation parameter?
ask.why: The Lagrange remainder uses an intermediate point determined by the increment.

steps.note: Replace the endpoint values.
The linear term uses the base-point gradient.
The quadratic remainder is evaluated along the segment.

ask.q: Can H_f(a + t*h) simply be replaced by H_f(a) without a remainder?
options: Not generally; a local remainder is needed
ask.why: For C² functions the replacement gives an o(‖h‖²) error; it is exact for constant Hessians.

cards.title: The local expansion at the base point
cards.body: For C² functions the Hessian changes continuously, so replacing the intermediate Hessian by the base-point Hessian creates a term negligible compared with ‖h‖².

cards.title: Keep the cross-term coefficient correct
cards.body: All displayed derivatives are at a. The mixed term appears twice inside the quadratic form and is multiplied by the overall 1/2.

cards.title: Exact quadratic example
cards.body: For f(x,y) = x² + xy + 2y², this is exact because the Hessian is constant. At h = (1,2), the value is 11.

cards.q: For a general C² scalar function, where is the Hessian evaluated in the exact Lagrange remainder?
options: At some intermediate point a + th
At any point outside the domain
cards.why: The exact second-order remainder uses an intermediate point; a base-point Hessian needs a small-o error term.

cards.q: For \(f=x^2+xy+2y^2\), calculate its exact quadratic value at (1,2).
cards.why: Substitution gives 1 + 2 + 8 = 11.

cards.q: Why is the simple mean value equality unsafe for vector outputs?
options: Different output components may require different intermediate points
The input must have dimension one
cards.why: Componentwise scalar theorems do not guarantee one common parameter for all components.

cards.title: Eigenvalues · curvature along special directions
cards.meaning: An eigenvalue is the multiplier by which a matrix scales a corresponding nonzero eigenvector.
cards.picture: A symmetric Hessian has perpendicular eigenvector directions. In those coordinates, its quadratic form contains separate squared coordinates with the eigenvalues as coefficients.
cards.example: The Hessian with rows (4,2) and (2,4) has eigenvalue 6 along (1,1), and eigenvalue 2 along (1,−1).
cards.bridge: For a unit eigenvector q, qᵀHq equals its eigenvalue, directly connecting eigenvalues and directional curvature.

cards.label: CO · 4 of 8 · 18 min
cards.title: What are an eigenvalue and eigenvector?
cards.body: An eigenvector is a nonzero direction that a matrix sends onto its own line. Its eigenvalue is the scalar multiplier in that action.

cards.title: Solve the characteristic equation
cards.body: Set the determinant to zero, giving λ = 2 and λ = 6. These are real because H is a real symmetric matrix.

cards.title: Check the directions explicitly
cards.body: Both vectors are nonzero and satisfy the eigenvector relation. Divide by √2 to make each have unit length.

cards.title: Quadratic form · one number from a direction
cards.meaning: A quadratic form is the scalar hᵀHh obtained by placing a vector on both sides of a matrix.
cards.picture: The matrix first transforms h; taking a dot product with h then measures the response along the original direction.
cards.example: For H = diag(2,−3), the value is 2h₁² − 3h₂², positive along one axis and negative along the other.
cards.bridge: In eigenvector coordinates a symmetric quadratic form becomes a sum of eigenvalues times squared coordinates.

cards.title: Diagonalise without changing lengths
cards.body: The spectral theorem supplies an orthogonal Q. Since ‖Qy‖ = ‖y‖, signs and bounds can be read from the eigenvalues in these coordinates.

cards.title: What do the curvature signs mean?
cards.body: Positive definite means every nonzero direction has positive quadratic form; negative definite means every such value is negative. Indefinite means both signs occur.

cards.title: Semidefinite permits a flat direction
cards.body: This matrix is positive semidefinite, not positive definite. Every vector (0,t) has zero quadratic form. A zero eigenvalue leaves that direction unresolved by the Hessian.

cards.title: The extreme eigenvalues bound the form
cards.body: For the matrix with eigenvalues 2 and 6, the form lies between 2‖h‖² and 6‖h‖². A determinant by itself does not give these individual curvature signs in dimensions above two.

cards.q: Find the smaller eigenvalue of \(\begin{pmatrix}4&2\\2&4\end{pmatrix}\).
cards.why: The characteristic polynomial is (λ − 2)(λ − 6), so the smaller root is 2.

cards.q: A real symmetric Hessian has eigenvalues −2, 0 and 5. What is its quadratic-form type?
cards.why: The positive and negative eigenvalues give directions with opposite signs, even though another direction has zero curvature.

cards.q: Why does a zero Hessian eigenvalue require caution?
options: It gives a direction whose quadratic term is zero
It makes all first partials vanish
It forces a saddle in every case
cards.why: Higher-order behaviour can decide what happens along a direction the quadratic approximation does not distinguish.

cards.title: Classification · look around, not just at the slope
cards.meaning: Classifying a stationary point means deciding whether nearby values rise, fall or do both relative to its value.
cards.picture: A bowl rises in every small nonzero direction, a cap falls, and a saddle rises in some directions while falling in others.
cards.example: At zero, x² + y² has a minimum, −x² − y² has a maximum, and x² − y² has a saddle.
cards.bridge: For C² functions the Hessian decides the strict-sign cases. Flat quadratic directions can require higher-order analysis.

cards.label: CO · 5 of 8 · 24 min
cards.title: What are a minimum, maximum and saddle?
cards.body: A local minimum has no smaller nearby values; a local maximum has no larger nearby values. A saddle has both larger and smaller values arbitrarily close to its stationary point.

cards.title: Look at signs around the same zero value
cards.body: For x² + y² every nearby nonzero value is positive. Its negative gives a maximum. For x² − y², horizontal displacements give positive values and vertical displacements give negative ones.

cards.title: Begin with stationarity and regularity
cards.body: Under these assumptions, a positive definite Hessian gives a strict local minimum, a negative definite Hessian gives a strict local maximum, and an indefinite Hessian gives a saddle.

cards.title: Why positive definiteness is sufficient
cards.body: If the smallest eigenvalue is positive, the quadratic term is bounded below by a positive multiple of ‖h‖². For sufficiently small nonzero h it dominates the remainder, making the difference positive.

cards.title: The two-variable determinant test
cards.body: At a stationary C² point: D > 0 with fₓₓ > 0 gives a strict minimum; D > 0 with fₓₓ < 0 gives a strict maximum; D < 0 gives a saddle. D = 0 is inconclusive.

cards.title: Find all stationary candidates
cards.body: The equations give y = x² and x = y², hence x⁴ = x. Over the reals this gives x = 0 or 1, and the candidates are (0,0) and (1,1).

cards.title: Classify the origin
cards.body: The negative determinant gives eigenvalues of opposite signs, so (0,0) is a saddle point.

cards.title: Classify the second candidate
cards.body: The Hessian is positive definite, so (1,1) is a strict local minimum. This does not make it a global minimum: along x = y = −t the cubic tends to −∞.

cards.title: A semidefinite Hessian can hide different outcomes
cards.body: f₊ has a strict minimum at zero. f₋ has a saddle, since values along the two axes have opposite signs. The same semidefinite Hessian cannot classify both.

cards.title: Even the zero Hessian allows several outcomes
cards.body: All have zero gradient and zero Hessian at the origin. They give a strict minimum, a strict maximum and a saddle, respectively.

cards.title: Do not omit the first-order test
cards.body: A positive definite Hessian at a point does not itself make the point a minimum. For f(x) = x + x² at zero, f″ = 2 but f′ = 1, so the point is not stationary.

cards.title: Singular does not always mean a saddle test fails
cards.body: A zero eigenvalue makes a purely semidefinite test inconclusive. If other eigenvalues already include both signs, the Hessian is indefinite and still proves a saddle.

cards.q: At a stationary point let \(f_{xx}=4\), \(f_{xy}=2\), \(f_{yy}=3\). Calculate D.
cards.why: D = 4·3 − 2² = 8; since fₓₓ > 0, the point is a strict local minimum under the C² hypothesis.

cards.q: At a C² stationary point the Hessian is diag(2,0). What conclusion follows from this Hessian alone?
cards.why: Both x² + y⁴ and x² − y⁴ have this Hessian at zero but different local behaviour.

cards.q: A C² stationary point has an indefinite Hessian with eigenvalues −1, 0 and 2. What is it?
options: Impossible because the determinant is zero
cards.why: Opposite-sign eigenvalues already give increasing and decreasing directions. A zero eigenvalue does not erase those directions.

sections.title: Convex Optimization · Convex sets and generalized order

sheets.title: Affine and convex sets
sheets.source: Boyd & Vandenberghe §§2.1–2.2, printed pp.21–35; FYUGP Module II, Unit 9.

cards.title: Convex set · straight travel stays inside
cards.meaning: A convex set is a collection of points containing the whole straight segment between any two of its points.
cards.picture: Choose two points anywhere in the region and stretch a straight string between them. No part of the string may leave the region.
cards.example: A filled disk is convex. A circle's outline is not: a chord passes through points missing from the outline.
cards.bridge: The allowed segment points are convex combinations θx + (1 − θ)y with 0 ≤ θ ≤ 1.

cards.label: CO · 6 of 8 · 24 min
cards.title: What is a convex set?
cards.body: A convex set contains every segment joining two of its points. A convex combination is a weighted average with nonnegative coefficients adding to one.

cards.title: A filled disk versus its outline
cards.body: The highlighted segment stays inside the filled disk. For the circle outline, the segment's interior is missing. Convexity concerns the whole set, not a boundary's appearance.
cards.art: <svg viewBox="0 0 260 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" aria-label="A filled disk contains a chord but a circle outline does not"><circle cx="66" cy="80" r="44" class="s ok"/><line x1="30" y1="55" x2="102" y2="105" class="hk" stroke-width="3"/><circle cx="193" cy="80" r="44" class="lk" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="157" y1="55" x2="229" y2="105" class="gk" stroke-width="2" stroke-dasharray="4 4"/><text x="66" y="151" class="t" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13">Filled: convex</text><text x="193" y="151" class="t" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13">Outline: not convex</text></svg>

cards.title: Affine set · keep the whole line
cards.meaning: An affine set contains the entire line through any two of its points, extending past both endpoints.
cards.picture: Convexity keeps the segment. Affineness also allows continuing beyond either end with negative or greater-than-one coefficients.
cards.example: The line x + y = 1 is affine and convex. A finite segment of that line is convex but not affine unless it is a single point.
cards.bridge: An affine combination requires coefficients adding to one but does not require them to be nonnegative.

cards.title: What is an affine set?
cards.body: An affine set contains all affine combinations of its points: the coefficients add to one and may be negative. Every affine set is convex; the converse does not hold.

cards.title: A linear equality defines an affine set
cards.body: If x and y solve Ax = b, every affine combination does too. Such a nonempty solution set is a translated subspace; it need not contain the origin.

cards.title: What are affine and convex hulls?
cards.body: The affine hull is the smallest affine set containing given points. The convex hull is the smallest convex set containing them. They collect the corresponding finite combinations.

cards.title: Two points give different hulls
cards.body: For distinct a and b, the convex hull is their segment and the affine hull is their whole line. Three noncollinear planar points have a filled triangle as convex hull and the whole plane as affine hull.

cards.title: What is affine dimension?
cards.body: Affine dimension is the dimension of the affine hull. A nontrivial segment has affine dimension one. A circle's affine hull is the plane, so its affine dimension is two despite its curve-like shape.

cards.title: What is relative interior?
cards.body: Relative interior means interior within a set's affine hull. A nontrivial line segment has empty interior in the plane, but its points other than the endpoints form its relative interior.

cards.title: What is a convex cone?
cards.body: A cone is closed under nonnegative scaling. A convex cone also permits addition, so it contains all conic combinations: sums with nonnegative coefficients and no sum-to-one restriction.

cards.title: Three coefficient rules
cards.body: Do not impose the convex sum-to-one condition on a conic combination. A union of two distinct rays can be a cone without being convex, because addition can leave the union.

cards.title: What are hyperplanes and halfspaces?
cards.body: A hyperplane satisfies aᵀx = b with nonzero a; a closed halfspace satisfies aᵀx ≤ b. Intersections of finitely many such sets are polyhedra. All these sets are convex.

cards.title: Common convex examples
cards.body: These are a norm ball, the probability simplex, and the second-order cone. Balls follow from the triangle inequality; the simplex is an intersection of linear constraints.

cards.title: An ellipsoid is an affine image of a ball
cards.body: For P = diag(4,1), E is (x₁ − a₁)²/4 + (x₂ − a₂)² ≤ 1, with semi-axis lengths 2 and 1. Scaling the unit disk by diag(2,1) and translating by a gives this convex ellipse.

cards.title: Symmetric positive semidefinite matrices form a cone
cards.body: For X,Y in this set and α,β ≥ 0, vᵀ(αX + βY)v is a nonnegative sum. Hence the PSD matrices form a convex cone in the vector space of symmetric matrices.

cards.q: Which planar set is convex but not affine?
options: A nonempty solution set Ax = b
cards.why: A segment contains the straight route between its points, but does not allow arbitrary extension beyond its endpoints.

cards.q: For a = (0,0), b = (4,2), find the first coordinate of \((1/4)a+(3/4)b\).
cards.why: The weighted average is (3, 1.5). The coefficients are nonnegative and sum to one.

cards.q: Which coefficient rule describes a conic combination?
options: Coefficients add to one, with arbitrary signs
Nonnegative coefficients, without a sum-to-one requirement
Coefficients are nonpositive and sum to zero
cards.why: Conic combinations permit any nonnegative scaling and addition.

sheets.title: Operations preserving convexity
sheets.source: Boyd & Vandenberghe §2.3, printed pp.35–42; FYUGP Module II, Unit 10.

cards.title: Convexity operations · build without losing segments
cards.meaning: A convexity-preserving operation constructs a new convex set from existing convex sets under stated conditions.
cards.picture: An affine map carries weighted averages to the same weighted averages. Intersections keep a segment because every participating set already contains it.
cards.example: Intersecting two disks is convex; taking their union can leave a gap. Projecting a convex solid onto a coordinate plane keeps a convex image.
cards.bridge: Perspective and linear-fractional maps also preserve convexity on a positive-denominator domain, even though they need not preserve the original segment parameter.

cards.label: CO · 7 of 8 · 20 min
cards.title: Intersections preserve convexity
cards.body: An intersection of any family of convex sets is convex. If two endpoints lie in every set, their entire segment lies in every set and therefore in the intersection.

cards.title: A union need not preserve convexity
cards.body: Each singleton is convex, but their union is not. This single missing midpoint disproves convexity; no complicated drawing is required.

cards.title: What is an affine map?
cards.body: An affine map has the form F(x) = Ax + b. It sends an affine combination of inputs to the same affine combination of their outputs, so it preserves convex images.

cards.title: Why an affine image of a convex set is convex

phases.name: Conclude

ask.why: Membership in the image means being the output of some input in C.

The coefficients on b add to one.

ask.why: θb + (1 − θ)b = b.

Convexity gives z ∈ C.

ask.why: z is precisely a convex combination of two members of C.

steps.note: Thus w lies in F(C), proving image convexity.

ask.q: Was injectivity or an inverse matrix needed?
options: Yes, det A must be positive
ask.why: The proof uses only the affine formula and convexity of C.

cards.title: What is an inverse image?
cards.body: F⁻¹(C) is the set of all inputs sent into C. It requires no inverse function. The inverse image of a convex set under an affine map is convex.

cards.title: Useful consequences of affine preservation
cards.tex: C+D=\{x+y:x\in C,y\in D\},\qquad C\times D=\{(x,y):x\in C,y\in D\}
cards.body: Cartesian products of convex sets are convex. Applying a sum map gives a convex Minkowski sum. Translations, arbitrary scalar multiples and coordinate projections also preserve convexity.

cards.title: What is a perspective map?
cards.body: The perspective map P(x,t) = x/t divides coordinates by a strictly positive last coordinate. Its images and inverse images preserve convexity on that domain.

cards.title: The segment weights change
cards.body: For t,s > 0 and θ in [0,1], μ stays in [0,1]. As θ ranges over the segment, μ does too. Thus a segment maps onto a segment, though generally with a different parametrization.

cards.title: Check the weights numerically
cards.body: The endpoint images are 2 and 0, whose equal-weight average would be 1. The correct output is their 1/4–3/4 combination, namely 1/2.

cards.title: What is a linear-fractional map?
cards.body: A linear-fractional map is an affine numerator divided by a positive affine denominator. It is an affine map followed by perspective, so it preserves convex images and inverse images on its domain.

cards.title: Keep the denominator restriction
cards.body: The denominator is positive throughout the interval, so the image is convex. The perspective theorem cannot simply be applied across a zero denominator or across both signs.

cards.q: Which construction always preserves convexity?
options: Removing the centre of a ball
cards.why: Every set in the intersection contains the segment between shared endpoints.

cards.q: For perspective P(x,t) = x/t, calculate \(P(\frac12(2,1)+\frac12(0,3))\).
cards.why: The midpoint input is (1,2), so its perspective is 1/2. Averaging endpoint images with the original equal weights would be wrong.

cards.q: What must be checked before applying the linear-fractional convexity theorem?
options: The denominator is positive on the considered domain
cards.why: The theorem uses the positive-coordinate domain of the perspective map.

sheets.title: Generalized inequalities
sheets.source: Boyd & Vandenberghe §2.4, printed pp.43–46; FYUGP Module II, Unit 11.

cards.title: Generalized order · choose the allowed positive differences
cards.meaning: A generalized inequality compares two vectors by asking whether their difference belongs to a chosen proper cone.
cards.picture: The cone is a collection of allowed nonnegative directions. Moving from x to y inside that cone means y is at least x in the chosen order.
cards.example: For the nonnegative orthant, (1,2) is below (3,4) because their difference is (2,2). But (1,3) and (2,2) are incomparable.
cards.bridge: For symmetric matrices, positive semidefinite differences replace nonnegative coordinate differences.

cards.label: CO · 8 of 8 · 22 min
cards.title: What is a proper cone?
cards.body: A proper cone is convex and closed, has nonempty interior (solid), and contains no nonzero vector together with its negative (pointed). The chosen ambient space matters.

cards.title: Examples and failures of properness
cards.tex: \mathbb R_+^n\text{ is proper};\qquad\mathbb R^n\text{ is not pointed}\ (n\ge1)
cards.body: A single ray in the plane has empty planar interior, so it is not solid there. The PSD cone is proper in the space of symmetric matrices, with positive definite matrices as its interior.

cards.title: What is a generalized inequality?
cards.body: For a proper cone K, x ≼ₖ y means y − x belongs to K. The strict relation x ≺ₖ y means y − x lies in the interior of K.
cards.tex: x\preceq_K y\iff y-x\in K,\qquad x\prec_K y\iff y-x\in\operatorname{int}K

cards.title: The nonnegative orthant gives coordinate comparisons
cards.tex: x\preceq_{\mathbb R_+^n}y\iff x_i\le y_i\text{ for every }i
cards.body: Here (1,2) ≼ (3,4). In contrast, neither (1,3) ≼ (2,2) nor (2,2) ≼ (1,3), because each comparison has one coordinate going the wrong way.

cards.title: Strict order is stronger than unequal weak order
cards.body: The difference (1,0) lies on the boundary of the orthant, not in its interior. Strict componentwise order requires every coordinate difference to be positive.

cards.title: What is a partial order?
cards.body: A partial order is reflexive, transitive and antisymmetric. Generalized cone order has these properties, but some pairs of points may be incomparable.

cards.title: Why cone properties supply order properties
cards.tex: y-x\in K,\ z-y\in K\ \Longrightarrow\ z-x=(z-y)+(y-x)\in K
cards.body: A convex cone is closed under addition, giving transitivity. Zero gives reflexivity. Pointedness gives antisymmetry: if a difference and its negative lie in K, the difference is zero.

cards.title: Addition, scaling and limits
cards.tex: x\preceq_K y,\ u\preceq_K v\ \Longrightarrow\ x+u\preceq_K y+v;\qquad\alpha x\preceq_K\alpha y\ (\alpha\ge0)
cards.body: Closedness of K also preserves weak inequalities under limits of both sides. Strict inequalities need positive scaling, and may become weak at a limit.

cards.title: What is Loewner matrix order?
cards.body: For real symmetric X and Y, X ≼ Y means Y − X is positive semidefinite. The strict relation means the difference is positive definite, rather than positive in each entry.

cards.title: A valid order despite negative entries
cards.body: The difference has eigenvalues 0 and 2, so X ≼ Y but not X ≺ Y. Its negative off-diagonal entries do not invalidate Loewner order.

cards.title: What are minimum and minimal elements?
cards.body: A minimum element is below every member of the set. A minimal element has no distinct member below it. A minimum is unique if it exists; several incomparable minimal elements can exist.

cards.title: Two minimal elements, no minimum
cards.body: Neither point is below the other, so both are minimal but neither is a minimum. Adding (0,0) creates one minimum and removes the other two from the minimal list.

cards.title: Incomparability versus one common minimum
cards.body: On the left, A and B are both minimal because neither dominates the other. On the right, the added origin is below both, becoming the unique minimum of the three-point set.

cards.title: The cone pictures of minimum and minimal
cards.tex: x\text{ minimum}\iff S\subseteq x+K,\qquad x\text{ minimal}\iff(x-K)\cap S=\{x\}
cards.body: The point x must itself belong to S. The first condition puts every set member above x; the second only rules out a distinct member below x. Maximum and maximal reverse the inequalities.

cards.title: Ordinary order is the special one-dimensional case
cards.body: For K = ℝ₊, generalized order is ordinary real-number order and all pairs are comparable. Minimum and minimal then agree. With vector orders, incomparability separates the notions.

cards.q: In componentwise order, compare x = (1,3) and y = (2,2).
cards.why: The first coordinate favours x ≼ y, but the second favours the reverse. Neither comparison holds in every coordinate.

cards.q: How many minimal elements does \(\{(0,1),(1,0)\}\) have under componentwise order?
cards.why: Neither member has a distinct member below it, so both are minimal. There is no minimum element.

cards.q: Which condition defines X ≼ Y in Loewner order for real symmetric matrices?
options: Every entry of Y − X is nonnegative
cards.why: Loewner order is induced by the PSD cone, so all quadratic forms of the difference must be nonnegative.
